title: The Death of Saul on Mount Gilboa
summary: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa, kill Saul's sons, and wound Saul, who dies by his own sword rather than fall into their hands. The Philistines display his armor and head in their temples, and the men of Jabesh-gilead recover and bury the bodies. The Chronicler closes with a verdict: Saul died for his unfaithfulness, because he did not keep the LORD's word, consulted a medium, and did not seek the LORD, so the LORD turned the kingdom over to David.
story: After nine chapters of genealogy, the narrative begins, and it begins with an ending. The Chronicler tells nothing of Saul's anointing, his early victories, or his long conflict with David, all of which fill 1 Samuel. He tells only Saul's death. The effect is stark: the first king of Israel appears in the story at the moment he falls, and the chapter exists to explain why the kingdom passed to David. Everything that follows in 1 Chronicles is David's story. This chapter clears the stage and gives the reason, in the Chronicler's own words, why the stage needed clearing.
historical:
Saul's death is usually placed around 1010 BC, though dates for this period are approximate. The account follows 1 Samuel 31 closely. Mount Gilboa rises at the south-east edge of the Jezreel Valley, the broad plain that cuts across northern Israel. The Philistines, who controlled the coastal plain in the south-west and whose iron weapons and organized armies had pressed Israel for generations, had pushed far north to fight there, cutting the central hill country off from the northern tribes. After the defeat, Israelites in the valley abandoned their towns (verse 7), and Philistine power reached deep into Israel.

The Chronicler shortens and adjusts some details. First Samuel 31:10 says the Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth-shan; Chronicles instead mentions his head in the temple of Dagon, the chief Philistine god, whose temples at Gaza and Ashdod appear in Judges 16 and 1 Samuel 5. The men of Jabesh-gilead had good reason to honor Saul: his first act as king had been to rescue their town from the Ammonites (1 Samuel 11).
cultural:
In ancient warfare a defeated king's body was a trophy. Stripping the dead, displaying the enemy's armor in a temple, and exhibiting his head proclaimed that the victors' gods had triumphed over the gods of the defeated. That is why the Philistines sent word to the temple of their idols (verse 9). Saul's fear of being tortured by the uncircumcised (verse 4) reflects the real cruelty with which captured kings were often treated. Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Israel (Genesis 17), and uncircumcised became a term for those outside that covenant, especially the Philistines.

Proper burial mattered deeply in Israel. To be left unburied was a disgrace and a curse, so the men of Jabesh-gilead risked their lives to recover the bodies, buried them under a tree, and fasted seven days, the customary period of mourning. Consulting a medium, a person who claimed to call up the spirits of the dead, was forbidden in Israel's law (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and Saul himself had earlier expelled mediums from the land (1 Samuel 28:3).
literary: The chapter is short and tightly built. Verses 1 to 12 are narrative, closely following 1 Samuel 31. Verses 13 and 14 are the Chronicler's own interpretation, and they are among the most important verses in the book because they set out his theology in miniature. Saul was unfaithful (maal), he did not keep the word of the LORD, he consulted a medium, and he did not seek (darash) the LORD. So the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom to David. The verdict also has a wordplay: Saul's name, Shaul, comes from the verb shaal, to ask, and he is condemned for asking (shaal) a medium instead of seeking the LORD. Verse 6 summarizes with finality that Saul died with all his house.

outline.t: Defeat on Mount Gilboa and the deaths of Saul and his sons
The Philistines occupy Israel's towns and dishonor Saul's body
The men of Jabesh-gilead bury Saul and his sons
The verdict: Saul's unfaithfulness and the kingdom turned to David

doctrines.note: The Chronicler says plainly that the LORD put Saul to death. The Philistines were the instruments, and Saul's own sword the means, but the ultimate cause was God's judgment on a king who would not keep his word or seek him.
The LORD turned the kingdom over to David. The transfer of power in Israel is presented not as the outcome of battle or politics but as God's decision.
Saul's turning to a medium is named as one of the reasons for his fall. Seeking guidance from the dead, or from any source in place of God, is treated as a betrayal of the covenant relationship.

words.note: Darash, to seek or inquire. It is perhaps the single most important verb in Chronicles. To seek the LORD means to turn to him in worship, prayer, and obedience, to make him one's first resort. The verb appears twice here: in verse 13 Saul sought guidance from the medium, and in verse 14 he did not seek the LORD. He was seeking, but in the wrong place. The good kings who follow will be measured by whether they sought him.

Maal, to act unfaithfully, used here with its related noun: literally, Saul was unfaithful with the unfaithfulness he committed. The doubled expression emphasizes the seriousness of his betrayal. It is the same word used for Judah's sin that led to exile (9:1).
Shaal, to ask. The name Saul (Shaul) means asked for, and the Chronicler uses this verb for his consulting the medium. The man whose name meant asked for asked the wrong source.

Ov, medium, one who claims to consult the spirits of the dead. The word may originally refer to the spirit itself or to a pit used in rituals. The law forbade such practices because they sought knowledge and power apart from God.

christ: Saul was the king the people asked for, chosen from among them and impressive to look at, and he failed because he would not keep God's word or seek God. His death opens the way for David, the king after God's own heart. The Bible's whole story of kingship runs from this failure toward a king who would be perfectly faithful. The New Testament presents Jesus as that king, the son of David who kept his Father's word completely and sought his will even in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39). The contrast is stark: Saul died for his own unfaithfulness; Jesus died for the unfaithfulness of others. This is a connection of theme and pattern, not a prediction in the chapter, but it shows why the story needed a better king than Saul.

hard.q: The Chronicler says Saul did not inquire of the LORD, but 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul inquired and the LORD did not answer. Do the accounts contradict each other?
hard.a: First Samuel 28:6 says Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets. First Chronicles 10:14 says he failed to inquire of the LORD. Interpreters handle this in several ways. Many note that the two books use different verbs: Samuel uses shaal (to ask), while Chronicles uses darash (to seek), which in Chronicles has a deeper meaning of wholehearted devotion. On this reading, Saul asked for information in a crisis but never sought the LORD in the covenant sense of turning to him in obedience and trust; his quick move to a medium when God was silent shows where his heart lay. Others see the Chronicler giving a summary verdict on Saul's whole reign rather than on one moment. Either way, the Chronicler is not denying that Saul made an inquiry; he is judging that Saul's life was not one of seeking God.

questions: The Chronicler sums up Saul's reign in two verses: unfaithfulness and failing to seek the LORD. If your life were summed up in two verses, what would they say?
When God seemed silent, Saul turned to a forbidden source of guidance. Where are you tempted to look for direction or comfort when God doesn't answer as quickly as you want?
The men of Jabesh-gilead remembered Saul's kindness to them years before and risked their lives to honor him. How do you honor people who once helped you, even after they have fallen?
